problem: The answer is technically wrong for the example given. Under the standard copy-restore scheme the address of each actual is fixed at the call, so swap(i, A[i]) with i = 1 and A = [10,20,30,40] gives i = 10, A[1] = 1 under call by reference AND under call by value-result. The two copy-outs also go to different variables (i and A[1]), so 'the second copy-out overwrites the first' never happens here. The real divergence for swap(i, A[i]) is between call by name and call by reference, because the name parameter re-evaluates A[i] after i has changed.
fix: Replace the question and answer. Correct answer: 'Call by reference and call by value-result agree on swap(i, A[i]), because both fix the address of A[1] at the call. Call by name differs: p = p + 1 becomes A[i] = A[i] + 1 with the new i. Reference and value-result differ when a formal aliases storage the callee also writes, e.g. with a global g, procedure f(int a) { g = 5; a = a + 1; } called as f(g): by reference g ends as 6, by value-result g ends as (old g) + 1.'

problem: The example is wrong. swap(i, A[i]) is not an aliasing case (i and A[1] are different locations, both addresses are fixed at the call), so call by reference and call by value-result give the same answer there; only call by name differs. The sentence also says 'the order of the writes', but for value-result the callee's write order is irrelevant - the copy-out order is what matters.
fix: Rewrite: 'Call by reference and call by value-result print the same answer unless a formal aliases storage the callee also writes. Example: a global g and procedure f(int a) { g = 5; a = a + 1; } called as f(g) - by reference g = 6, by value-result g = (old g) + 1. When two formals alias one variable, as in p(x, x) with body a = 1; b = 2, the copy-out order decides the value. Call by name is the mechanism that changes swap(i, A[i]), because A[i] is re-evaluated after i changes.'

problem: The claim 'A generic method is instantiated once per type it is used with, one copy of the code for int and another for String' is true for C++ templates but false for Java, which this paragraph is describing. Java generics use type erasure: one copy of the method is compiled for all type arguments, and casts are inserted where needed.
fix: 'A C++ template method is instantiated once per type it is used with, one copy of the code for int and another for String. A Java generic method is erased instead: a single copy of the code serves all type arguments, with casts inserted at the call sites.'

problem: 'C passes scalars by value and arrays by reference' contradicts the standard statement that C has only call by value. What is passed is a pointer to the first element, itself passed by value. The next clause gives the right mechanism, but the opening phrase is the one a student will memorise.
fix: 'C passes every argument by value. For an array, the array name decays to the address of its first element, so passing it copies one word, a pointer, not the array; the callee can still change the elements through that pointer.'

where: Section 2, call by name bullet (Jensen's device)
problem: Passing i as a name parameter is only half of Jensen's device. The summed expression a[i] must also be passed by name, otherwise the trick does not work: the callee's loop changes i, and the term re-evaluates with the current i.
fix: 'Jensen's device is the classic use: Sum(i, 1, n, a[i]) passes both the loop variable i and the term a[i] by name, so the callee's loop drives the caller's i and a[i] is re-evaluated for each value of i.'

problem: 'The order of the writes then decides the answer' is right for call by reference but misleading for value-result, where the writes inside the callee touch private copies; it is the order of the copy-outs at return that decides.
fix: 'With reference or value-result, two formals can name the same variable. For reference the order of the writes decides the answer; for value-result the order of the copy-outs at return decides it.'
